chunks: Zur'ah narrated from Sama'ah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
Two men disputed before ʿAlī عليه السلام over a beast, and each one of them claimed that it was born at his manger. Each one of them produced evidence equal in number.
So he drew lots between them with two lots, and he marked the two lots for each one of them with a distinguishing sign, then he said:

O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens, Lord of the seven earths, and Lord of the Mighty Throne, Knower of the unseen and the seen, the All-beneficent, the All-merciful, whichever of the two is the owner of the beast and has the stronger right to it, I ask You to bring forth his lot.
Then the lot of one of them came out, so he judged it to belong to him.

key_terms.اخْتَصَمَا: they entered into a dispute or litigation
key_terms.السَّهْمَيْنِ: the two lots used in the drawing
key_terms.دَابَّةٍ: a beast or riding animal that was the subject of the ownership dispute
key_terms.سَوَاءً: equal or matched, here in the number of proofs
key_terms.عَالِمَ الْغَيْبِ وَ الشَّهَادَةِ: Knower of the unseen and the seen, invoking Allah's complete knowledge
key_terms.فَأَقْرَعَ: he drew lots to determine the rightful claimant
key_terms.فَقَضَى: he rendered judgment or ruled legally

ai.seo_question: How did Imam ʿAlī عليه السلام judge a case when two people had equal evidence?
ai.summary: This hadith describes a judicial case before Imam ʿAlī عليه السلام in which two claimants presented equal evidence over ownership of an animal. When the proofs were evenly matched, he resorted to drawing lots accompanied by du'a to Allah, and then judged in favor of the one whose lot emerged. The report highlights judgment by lot as a means of resolving otherwise equal claims.
